title: What is the difference between a plain view (a stored query, computed on every access — always fresh, no storage) and a materialized view (a physical, stored snapshot refreshed periodically/on-demand — fast reads but can be stale), and when do you use each?
shortTitle: Plain View vs Materialized View — and When to Use Each

s1_definition.profdef: A plain (regular) view is a stored `SELECT` definition that is executed every time it is queried, so it holds no data and always reflects the current base tables, at the cost of re-running its query each access. A materialized view physically stores the query's result set on disk as a snapshot and serves that stored result quickly, but it can be stale and must be refreshed (on a schedule, on demand, or incrementally) to pick up base-table changes.
s1_definition.analogy: A plain view is like asking the clerk to recompute "total deposits per branch today" every single time you ask — always current, but you wait while they add it up. A materialized view is like a printed end-of-hour summary pinned to the wall: you read it instantly, but it only shows what was true when it was last printed, so it is fast yet possibly a little out of date until it is reprinted.
s1_definition.oneliner: A plain view recomputes live every access (fresh but slower); a materialized view stores a snapshot (fast but can be stale and needs refreshing).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A plain (regular) view is a stored `SELECT` definition that is executed every time it is queried, so it holds no data and always reflects the current base tables, at the cost of re-running its query each access. A materialized view physically stores the query's result set on disk as a snapshot and serves that stored result quickly, but it can be stale and must be refreshed (on a schedule, on demand, or incrementally) to pick up base-table changes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A plain view is like asking the clerk to recompute "total deposits per branch today" every single time you ask — always current, but you wait while they add it up. A materialized view is like a printed end-of-hour summary pinned to the wall: you read it instantly, but it only shows what was true when it was last printed, so it is fast yet possibly a little out of date until it is reprinted.

**One line to remember:** A plain view recomputes live every access (fresh but slower); a materialized view stores a snapshot (fast but can be stale and needs refreshing).

sections.s2_technical:
A plain view stores only its query text. When you `SELECT` from it, the database expands or merges the view's query into yours and executes it against the live base tables, so results are always consistent with the current data and no extra storage is used. The downside is that an expensive underlying query — heavy joins or aggregations over millions of rows — pays that full cost on every access, which is wasteful if the data changes rarely but is read constantly.

A materialized view executes its query once and stores the resulting rows physically, like a cached table. Reads then hit the stored snapshot and are fast, which is ideal for expensive aggregations in dashboards and reports. The trade-off is staleness and maintenance: the snapshot does not automatically track base-table changes, so you refresh it — a full refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the data, while some engines support incremental or "fast" refresh that applies only the deltas, and PostgreSQL offers `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` so reads are not blocked during refresh. You also spend disk on the stored result and must decide the refresh cadence (periodic schedule, on-demand, or triggered by data changes). Engine support varies: Oracle and PostgreSQL have first-class materialized views, SQL Server achieves the same effect with indexed views, and MySQL has no native materialized view so teams simulate one with a summary table plus a refresh job.

The decision rule is about the read-to-write ratio and freshness tolerance. Use a plain view when you need always-current data, the underlying query is cheap, writes are frequent relative to reads, or you simply want simplification, security, and abstraction without storage. Use a materialized view when the query is expensive, reads vastly outnumber writes, and the business can tolerate slightly stale data — classic cases are nightly analytics, branch dashboards, and precomputed aggregates. The senior framing is a trade-off between freshness and read speed: a plain view optimizes for correctness and zero storage, a materialized view optimizes for read latency at the cost of staleness and refresh overhead.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India has two reporting needs. The compliance screen must show the *current* balance of an account, which must never be stale, so it uses a plain view that recomputes live. The executive dashboard shows total deposits per branch across millions of transactions, an expensive aggregation read thousands of times an hour but tolerably accurate as of the last refresh, so it uses a materialized view refreshed every fifteen minutes.

Our mini-project models both: a `PlainView` that recomputes from the live base data every call (so later changes are immediately visible) and a `MaterializedView` that computes once, stores a snapshot (so later changes are NOT visible until refreshed), tracks a refresh timestamp, and exposes a `refresh()` method — demonstrating fresh-but-slower versus fast-but-stale.

```
materialized-view-demo/
└── src/main/java/com/nbi/db/

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions across two branches, with a materialized-view snapshot taken immediately at sequence zero.

Step 1 — Before any new deposit, both views agree: branch BR01 totals fifteen thousand, branch BR02 totals eight thousand, because the snapshot was just taken from the same data.

Step 2 — A new one-hundred-thousand deposit arrives in the base table for BR01 after the snapshot was taken.

Step 3 — The plain view is queried and immediately reflects the new deposit, showing BR01 at one hundred fifteen thousand, because it recomputes live against the base table every time.

Step 4 — The materialized view is queried and still shows the old fifteen thousand for BR01, because it serves the stored snapshot from sequence zero and has not seen the new deposit yet — this is the staleness trade-off in exchange for fast reads.

Step 5 — The scheduled fifteen-minute refresh runs, recomputing and replacing the snapshot, so the materialized view now also shows BR01 at one hundred fifteen thousand and records that it was refreshed at sequence fifteen.

Final output:

```text
Before new deposit:
  plain view (live)      = {BR01=15000.0, BR02=8000.0}
  materialized (snap @0) = {BR01=15000.0, BR02=8000.0}
After new 100000 deposit to BR01, BEFORE refresh:
  plain view (live)      = {BR01=115000.0, BR02=8000.0}   <- reflects new deposit (fresh)
  materialized (snap @0) = {BR01=15000.0, BR02=8000.0}   <- STALE, old snapshot
After REFRESH:
  materialized (snap @15) = {BR01=115000.0, BR02=8000.0}   <- now up to date
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  base: txns (branch, amount)  ← writes keep arriving
    │
    ├─ PLAIN VIEW ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    │    SELECT branch, SUM(amount) ... (runs EVERY query)
    │    read ─▶ always reflects latest base   [fresh, slower, no storage]
    │
    └─ MATERIALIZED VIEW ──────────────────────────────────────
         compute ONCE ─▶ [ stored snapshot on disk ]
         read ─▶ snapshot   [fast, but STALE until refresh]
         REFRESH (schedule/on-demand/incremental) ─▶ snapshot updated
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Choosing View Type by Read/Write & Freshness ═══

  ┌──────────────┐ needs CURRENT  ┌──────────────┐  live query  ┌──────────┐
  │ Compliance   │ ─────────────▶ │ PLAIN VIEW   │ ───────────▶ │ base     │
  │ screen       │  (never stale) │ (recompute)  │              │ tables   │
  └──────────────┘                └──────────────┘              └──────────┘

  ┌──────────────┐ tolerates lag  ┌───────────────┐  snapshot   ┌──────────┐
  │ Exec         │ ─────────────▶ │ MATERIALIZED  │ ◀─refresh──  │ base     │
  │ dashboard    │ (fast, heavy   │ VIEW (stored) │  every 15m   │ tables   │
  └──────────────┘  aggregation)  └───────────────┘              └──────────┘

  Rule: fresh+cheap+write-heavy → plain | expensive+read-heavy+lag-OK → materialized
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Two View Strategies ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: PlainView vs MaterializedView share a read interface    │
  │ Cache/Memoize: materialized view = refreshable cached result      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: plain recomputes; materialized stores+refreshes               │
  │ O: new refresh policy (incremental) = new method                 │
  │ L: both expose totalsPerBranch() interchangeably                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Plain vs Materialized ──
  PLAIN        : runs query each access | always fresh | no storage | slower if heavy
  MATERIALIZED : stored snapshot        | can be stale | uses disk   | fast reads
  REFRESH      : full | incremental/fast | CONCURRENTLY (non-blocking)
  ENGINES      : Oracle/PG native | SQL Server indexed view | MySQL = summary table

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → plain.totalsPerBranch()  [live recompute, always current]
  3.   base.add(new deposit)
  4.   → mat.totalsPerBranch()    [old snapshot, STALE]
  5.   → mat.refresh(15)          [recompute + replace snapshot]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A plain view and a materialized view trade freshness against read speed. A plain, regular view stores only its `SELECT` definition and executes it every time it is queried, so it never stores data and always reflects the current base tables, but it pays the full cost of its underlying query on every access, which is wasteful when that query is an expensive aggregation read very often. A materialized view executes its query once and physically stores the resulting rows as a snapshot, so reads are fast because they hit the stored result, but the snapshot can be stale and must be refreshed — fully, incrementally, or with PostgreSQL's non-blocking `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` — and it consumes disk space.

The decision rule I use is based on the read-to-write ratio and the tolerance for staleness. I use a plain view when the data must always be current, the underlying query is cheap, writes are frequent relative to reads, or I just want simplification, security, and abstraction without storing anything. I use a materialized view when the query is expensive, reads vastly outnumber writes, and the business can accept data that is accurate as of the last refresh. At the National Bank of India our compliance screen used a plain view so an account's current balance was never stale, while the executive dashboard used a materialized view of total deposits per branch over millions of transactions, refreshed every fifteen minutes, because that aggregation was read thousands of times an hour and a short lag was acceptable. A senior nuance I add is that engine support differs — Oracle and PostgreSQL have native materialized views, SQL Server uses indexed views, and MySQL has none, so you simulate one with a summary table and a refresh job — and that choosing the refresh cadence is itself a design decision balancing freshness against refresh cost. The line I always state is that a plain view recomputes live and is always fresh but slower, while a materialized view serves a stored snapshot that is fast but can be stale and must be refreshed.

keyPoints: Stored procedure: precompiled SQL code on the DB server
Views: virtual table from a SELECT — simplify complex queries
Pros: performance, security. Cons: hard to version, test, debug
